models.name: Helical Thread Sector (HTS) Model
models.what_it_computes: Local contact tractions and circumferential reaction moments on a periodic helical thread sector to recover incremental insertion torque versus axial advance under controlled frictional regimes.

models.name: Full-Screw Orthotropic Bone Block (FS-OB) Model
models.what_it_computes: Global torque–rotation response of a full 3D screw engaging an orthotropic cortical shell and crushable cancellous core, including peak seating torque and energy partition between contact slip and bone deformation.

models.name: Cohesive Interface Damage (CID) Model
models.what_it_computes: Torque evolution with progressive thread–bone interfacial degradation using cohesive traction–separation laws embedded along the flank contact, capturing post-peak torque decay and damage work.

mechanisms.name: Interfacial friction control
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Thread flank friction sets the dominant resistive moment during advance and governs sensitivity of insertion torque to lubrication and surface finish.

mechanisms.name: Cortical microcrushing at thread root
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Inelastic deformation and microcrack accumulation in cortex elevate torque near seating and influence long-term fixation quality.

mechanisms.name: Pilot-hole undersizing and thread forming
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Reduced pilot-hole diameter increases material flow and forming work at first engagement, shifting the torque–advance profile and peak levels.

mechanisms.name: Thermo-mechanical softening
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Frictional heat can reduce interfacial shear strength and cortical stiffness during steady advance, altering torque demand and stability.

deviation.detail: All credibility factors are scored per model–mechanism pair on a 0–7 Credibility Readiness Index (CRI), where 0 indicates no evidence and 7 indicates comprehensive evidence with demonstrated repeatability.

spans: For friction control regimes, the HTS achieved 6.0% MAPE averaged across dry, saline, and roughened conditions, with peak torques within 0.07 N·m of measured means.

Across 76 insertions performed in two laboratories with 3.5 mm self-tapping cortical screws (1.25 mm pitch), the HTS model reproduced friction-controlled torque increments with a mean absolute percent error (MAPE) of 6.0%, was sensitive to thermally induced changes in shear strength when modeled as a reduced friction proxy (MAPE 19.5%), and predicted the effect of 2.0 mm versus 2.4 mm pilot holes within 3.5% of the observed increase.

spans: Thermal imaging with 50 Hz infrared cameras and embedded micro-thermocouples recorded temperature rise of 14 ± 3 °C at 30 rpm and 22 ± 4 °C at 50 rpm under dry conditions; saline irrigation reduced these rises by approximately 40%.

spans: For the FS-OB model, the thermo-mechanical coupling used the same partition factor for heat to the cortex η = 0.85 as measured in tribometry under comparable slip rates, and conductivity, heat capacity, and density were set from published values for ovine cortical bone.
Parameter-transfer residuals in frictional dissipation per turn when matched to HTS were 2.8%, 3.5%, 2.9%, and 4.1% over the four mechanisms.

spans: The CID replaced classical contact at the thread flanks with a zero-thickness layer obeying a traction–separation law in mode II (tangential) with coupled damage initiated at τ0 and evolving over a critical slip δf to a residual τr.
This construction allowed us to capture post-peak torque decay as interfacial capacity diminished with slip and heating.

spans: Inputs were based on specimen-matched E values and cohesive strengths regressed from tribometry, not tuned to torque curves.
The CID model’s temperature dependence of cohesive work Wc(T) was obtained by regressing tribometer shear strength versus temperature, with β 0.015 K1 yielding correct slopes over 20–50 °C.
